title: Tenant fencing and fallback guidelines
content:
Purpose and context:
This is an engineering-first working note describing pragmatic options for tenant/org-aware routing, capacity fencing, and automated fallback strategies across regions and serving tiers. The goal is to produce a lightweight, operationally safe set of controls that map contract SLAs, billing tiers, and noisy-neighbor signals to runtime routing decisions.

Audience:
- Platform engineers implementing routing & policy enforcement
- SREs who will operate tenant fencing during incidents
- Solutions/Customer Success for request handling expectations

High-level requirements (from product/security/SRE):
- Enforce per-tenant throughput and burst limits in a way that prevents single customers from degrading others (noisy neighbor).
- Respect contract SLAs: latency targets, region affinity, dedicated vs shared pools.
- Allow graceful degradation (fallback to cheaper model, best-effort routing) rather than hard errors where possible.
- Low enforcement latency (policy decisions applied in <= 200ms path while cold starts allowed to be slower).
- Clear audit trail + observability for billing and debugging.

Terminology (working definitions):
- Tenant: billing/organization boundary (org_id).
- Tier: customer tier (free, standard, pro, enterprise).
- Pool: serving capacity grouping (shared, dedicated, reserved-region).
- Fencing: active controls that limit or isolate tenant traffic to protect others (throttles, route isolation, queue prioritization).
- Fallback: policy-driven downgrade actions applied when preferred route cannot satisfy SLOs (model downgrade, region fallback, best-effort queue).

Policy primitives we intend to support:
- Static quotas: per-minute token/request limits with fixed burst buckets.
- Sliding-window rate counters: more adaptive to spikes, backed by Redis or in-memory sharded counters for hot tenants.
- Latency/error triggers: detect noisy neighbor behavior using latency P95, error-rate thresholds over windows (e.g., P95 > 1.5x baseline or >10% errors).
- Affinity constraints: soft and hard region constraints driven by legal/privacy SLAs.
- Tier mappings: map tier -> default pools, max concurrency, preferred model families.
- Emergency tags: allow operators to pin tenants to isolation mode (manual or automated).

Routing decision model (request path outline):
1) Request arrives at edge with org_id, tier, route metadata (model, region hints).
2) Policy evaluation service (local cache) returns route decision: preferred pool, fallback list, quota tokens, and mitigation flags.
3) Serving runtime enforces quotas (fast path) and routes request to chosen pool; if chosen pool rejects due to local capacity, use fallback list before returning error.
4) Observability events emitted for each decision and enforcement action (decision_id, org_id, token_counts, latency_observed).

Control plane responsibilities:
- Authoritative store for tenant policies (Conductor DB) with versioning and rollout state.
- Expose read-optimized policy cache service (HTTP/gRPC) deployed co-located with edge nodes for <50ms lookup.
- Provide admin UI + API for overrides, emergency fencing, and SLA changes (audit-logged).
- Ship analytics pipeline for noisy neighbor detection (streaming signals -> anomalies -> automated mitigation).

Serving plane responsibilities:
- Enforce token/burst counters for per-tenant quotas (use per-worker counters with consistent hashing of org_id).
- Bulk-decisions use prepopulated fallback lists to avoid synchronous control plane hits on overload.
- Emit enforcement telemetry and allow operator-triggered rollbacks.

Fencing strategies (ordered from least to most disruptive):
- Soft deprioritization: reduce tenant priority in queueing/batching, allow best-effort completion.
- Model degrade: route to lighter/quantized model variant (explicit mapping by tier).
- Rate limit throttles: drop/queue requests above tier limits with explicit Retry-After headers.
- Isolation: move tenant traffic to dedicated pool (if available) or isolate on specific nodes.
- Hard cut: circuit-break to return 429/503 for abusive or runaway tenants (last resort).

Multi-region specifics and concerns:
- Affinity first: honor region constraints for enterprise customers unless emergency fallback allowed in contract.
- Cross-region fallback: define allowed fallback regions per-tenant; enabled only for transient outages and with billing/latency caveats surfaced to customers.
- Cold-start cost: moving traffic cross-region or to dedicated pools may trigger cold start. Use queued warmers for high-SLA tenants and predictive capacity for known patterns.
- Data residency: never route to non-authorized regions for tenants with residency restrictions.

Noisy neighbor detection heuristics (initial proposal):
- Combine token-rate surge (tokens/s > 3x baseline), sustained high P95 latency (>1.5x baseline for >= 2 mins), and error-rate (>5%) to mark a tenant as noisy.
- If 2/3 signals fire, start a mitigation workflow: issue soft deprioritization -> monitor for 30s -> escalate to rate-limits or model degrade if still noisy.
- Persist noisy flags for a short TTL (e.g., 5m) and escalate if recurrent across multiple windows.

Example policy DSL (human-readable pseudo-format):
- policy "enterprise-tier" {
    tier: "enterprise"
    quotas: { tokens_per_minute: 500000, burst: 20000 }
    preferred_pools: ["dedicated-eastus-1", "dedicated-europe-1"]
    fallback: ["shared-low-latency", "shared-cost-optimized"]
    region_policy: { allow_fallback: false }
  }

- policy "standard-tier" {
    tier: "standard"
    quotas: { tokens_per_minute: 50000, burst: 2000 }
    preferred_pools: ["shared-low-latency"]
    fallback: ["shared-cost-optimized"]
    region_policy: { allow_fallback: true }
  }

Operational playbook (quick start for SRE):
- Alert: noisy-tenant-detected (ticket auto-populates tenant id, recent P95, errors, token-rate).
- Triage: check policy version, recent rollouts, customer commit window (is there an ongoing large job?).
- Remediate: start with soft deprioritization via fast-flag; if persists >2 minutes, apply model degrade or temporary rate limit.
- Communicate: post to customer-success/channel with action taken and ETA.
- Postmortem: if tenant was misclassified, capture signal thresholds and adjust heuristics.

Testing plan and rollout:
- Unit test: policy evaluation logic, quota counter correctness, fallback sequence.
- Integration: synthetic tenant load tests verifying routing & enforcement across regions and pools.
- Chaos: inject region failure + capacity exhaustion to validate fallback ordering and SLA behavior.
- Staged rollout: start with low-impact tenants, enable canary for 5% of traffic, and monitor error-rate & latency deltas.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Enforcement locality vs centralization: full local enforcement reduces lookup latency but risks policy staleness; we need a hybrid TTL + invalidation model.
- Billing signal sync: how quickly should enforcement reflect billing-flag changes (e.g., suspended customer)? Near-realtime is desirable but may be expensive.
- Fairness across tiers: should free-tier throttles be bursty-friendly to allow faster UX for small spikes?
- Consistency model for counters: eventual counters are cheaper but can allow short-lived overages; do we accept some overage for lower tiers?

Short-term action items (next 2 weeks):
- PLAT-892: implement local policy cache with 60s TTL and invalidation hooks (owner: Liam).
- Prototype per-tenant sliding-window counters in Redis (owner: Maya).
- Add noisy-neighbor detection job to streaming pipeline; create dashboard (owner: Diego).
- Draft SLA-to-policy mapping doc for product/legal (owner: Asha).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Validate policy DSL with product to ensure expressiveness for contract clauses (data residency, compute isolation).
- Add example telemetry dashboard panels: tenant-level P95, token-usage, enforcement actions over time.
- Build a lightweight simulator to tune thresholds before enabling automated mitigations.

References and related docs:
- Confluence: Tenant Routing Design (linked above)
- Existing platform routing sketches (see platform repo PR 458)
- Customer incident notes: CS-2024-11 (noisy batch job that impacted shared pool)

Bottom line: implement a layered, minimally-volatile control plane that keeps fast-path enforcement local, exposes operator controls for emergency fencing, and prefers graceful fallbacks over hard errors. The design should be iterative: start with conservative detection and manual mitigations, then progressively automate as confidence grows.
